quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on the five terms that carry managerial accounting: cost object, accumulation, assignment, direct and indirect cost.

questions.q: A cost object is…
options: Anything — a product, machine, service or process — for which a separate measurement of cost is desired
The account in which costs are recorded
A fixed asset of the mill
questions.explain: A cost object is whatever the manager wants costed: a lot of fabric, a loom, a dyeing route, a customer order. It is not an account or an amount.

questions.q: Cost accumulation means…
options: Collecting cost data in some organised way, such as by department or machine
Adding a profit margin to cost
questions.explain: Accumulation is the collecting stage; assigning the collected costs to cost objects comes afterwards.

questions.q: Cost assignment covers which two activities?
options: Tracing and allocating the accumulated cost to the cost object
questions.explain: Assignment = tracing (direct costs) plus allocating (indirect costs). Recording and summarising belong to financial accounting.

questions.q: A direct cost is a cost related to the cost object that…
options: Can be traced to it in an economically feasible way
questions.explain: The test is economic traceability — the grey fabric in a dyeing lot, the yarn in a beam. Size, cash payment and behaviour with output are not the criteria.

questions.q: An indirect cost is one that…
options: Is unrelated to the cost object
Is related to the cost object but cannot be traced economically, so it is allocated
questions.explain: Indirect costs do relate to the object (the electricity did run the machine) but tracing them is not worth the effort, so a share is allocated instead.

questions.q: Managerial accounting mainly reports to owners, banks and the tax authority.
questions.explain: That is financial accounting, which looks backwards and outwards. Managerial accounting looks inwards, measuring the cost of the things managers decide about.

questions.q: With one dyeing order as the cost object, which of these is an indirect cost?
options: Grey fabric issued to the order
questions.explain: Steam serves every order at once and is allocated per metre. Fabric, dyes and chemicals weighed for the order are traced directly.

questions.q: The same cost can be direct for one cost object and indirect for another.
questions.explain: The loom-shed supervisor’s salary is direct to the weaving department but indirect to any single order woven there. Direct or indirect is a relationship, not a property of the cost.

questions.q: Financial accounting is described in the lecture as looking…
options: Backwards and outwards, reporting to owners, banks and the tax authority
questions.explain: Financial accounting reports past results to outsiders; managerial accounting looks inwards and forwards to decisions.

questions.q: The lecture’s advice when a cost figure looks ‘obvious’ is to ask…
questions.explain: An allocated figure rests on a chosen base and could be different under another base; a traced figure is a measurement. Knowing which you have is the first step in reading any cost.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: How allocation rates are built from a cost pool and a base, and how the choice of cost object changes what is direct.

questions.q: If the cost object is narrowed from the dyeing department to a single dyeing order, what happens?
questions.explain: The manager’s salary and the range’s depreciation are direct to the department but only allocated to one order. Narrower objects leave fewer costs that can be traced.

questions.q: Steam for the whole plant is allocated per metre. The allocation rate is…
options: Total steam cost × total metres processed
Total steam cost ÷ total metres processed
Steam cost of the largest order ÷ its metres
questions.explain: Rate = cost pool ÷ base, giving rupees per metre. The reversed formula gives metres per rupee, which is meaningless here.

questions.q: Plant steam costs Rs 450,000 in a month in which 150,000 metres are processed. What is the steam allocation rate per metre?
The depreciation of the pad-steam range is allocated to orders per machine-hour. The rate is…
questions.explain: Rupees per hour = cost pool ÷ hours. Dividing by the number of orders ignores that a long order uses the machine for more hours than a short one.

questions.q: Annual depreciation of a pad-steam range is Rs 1,200,000 and it runs 4,000 machine-hours a year. What is the depreciation rate per machine-hour?
questions.explain: 1,200,000 ÷ 4,000 = Rs 300 per machine-hour.

questions.q: Allocation assigns a cost to a cost object through a base such as metres or machine-hours, rather than by direct measurement.
questions.explain: Tracing measures the cost on the object itself; allocation spreads a pool across objects in proportion to a chosen base.

questions.q: A cost could in principle be traced to each order, but measuring it would cost more than the information is worth. It should be treated as…
options: A direct cost, because tracing is possible
An indirect cost, because tracing is not economically feasible
questions.explain: The definition of direct cost requires tracing in an economically feasible way. Where tracing is uneconomic the cost is allocated.

questions.q: If steam is allocated per metre and an order’s length doubles, the steam cost allocated to that order…
questions.explain: Allocated cost = rate × metres, so twice the metres receives twice the steam charge, whether or not the order actually used that much steam.

questions.q: The total direct cost of a dyeing order is…
options: The sum of all costs traced to it
The sum of all costs allocated to it
The department’s total cost ÷ number of orders
questions.explain: Direct cost is what can be traced — grey fabric, dyes, chemicals weighed for the order. Allocated items make up the indirect cost.

questions.q: Grey fabric issued to an order cost Rs 180,000, dyes Rs 22,500 and chemicals Rs 6,000, all weighed for the order. What is the total direct cost of the order?

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Build the cost of a dyeing order from its traced items and its allocated shares of steam, depreciation and supervision.

questions.q: An order of 2,500 metres is charged steam at an allocation rate of Rs 3 per metre. What is the steam cost allocated to the order?
Depreciation of the pad-steam range is allocated at Rs 300 per machine-hour and the order occupies the range for 6.5 hours. What depreciation is allocated to the order?
An order has direct costs of Rs 208,500, allocated steam Rs 7,500, allocated depreciation Rs 1,950 and allocated supervision Rs 4,200. What is its total cost?
An order costing Rs 222,150 in total is 2,500 metres long. What is the cost per metre, to the nearest paisa?
The dyeing manager’s salary of Rs 150,000 a month is direct to the department but is allocated equally to the 12 orders processed in the month. What share does each order receive?

Plant steam costs Rs 600,000 and is allocated to departments per metre. The dyeing department processed 120,000 of the plant’s 200,000 metres. How much steam cost is allocated to the dyeing department?
3,000 metres of grey fabric at Rs 65 per metre are issued to a dyeing order. What direct fabric cost is traced to the order?
questions.explain: 3,000 × 65 = Rs 195,000, traced directly from the issue note.

questions.q: 12 kg of dyes at Rs 1,850 per kg are weighed for a shade. The direct dye cost of the order is…
questions.explain: 12 × 1,850 = Rs 22,200. The other figures are arithmetic slips (12 × 1,835, 12 × 2,000).

questions.q: Electricity of Rs 2,400,000 a year is allocated over 8,000 machine-hours. An order uses the machine for 5 hours. What electricity cost is allocated to it?
A supervisor costing Rs 90,000 a month is allocated per metre over 150,000 metres. An order of 2,500 metres receives…
questions.explain: Rate = 90,000 ÷ 150,000 = Rs 0.60 per metre; 2,500 × 0.60 = Rs 1,500. Rs 600 is the rate in paisa misread as rupees.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Classify real mill costs for a dyeing order and a dyeing department, and spot where ‘obvious’ figures hide an allocation.

questions.q: Dyes are weighed out for the shade of a particular order. With that order as the cost object the dyes are…
options: Not a cost of the order
questions.explain: The dyes are weighed specifically for the order, so they are traced to it directly — direct for the order and for the department alike.

questions.q: Steam is raised in one boiler for the whole plant. With one dyeing order as the cost object, the steam is…
options: Direct, because the order used steam
questions.explain: The order did consume steam, but no one measures how much; the plant’s steam cost is allocated per metre. ‘Used it’ is not the same as ‘traced’.

questions.q: The dyeing manager’s salary is…
options: Direct to one order, indirect to the department
Indirect to one order, direct to the department
questions.explain: The salary is paid for running the department, so it is traced to it; a single order gets only an allocated share.

questions.q: Depreciation of the pad-steam range is classified as…
options: Direct to the order, indirect to the department
Indirect to the order (allocated per machine-hour), direct to the department
questions.explain: The range belongs to the dyeing department, so its depreciation is direct there; each order is charged a share per machine-hour.

questions.q: A loom-shed supervisor’s salary is a direct cost of each order woven in the shed.
questions.explain: The salary is direct to the weaving department but indirect to any one order; it must be allocated across the orders.

questions.q: The costing office is asked ‘what did order 4471 cost?’. What is the first step?
options: Add up all the department’s costs for the month
Define the cost object and decide which costs can be traced and which must be allocated
Take the selling price and deduct the margin
questions.explain: Costing starts by fixing the object and classifying costs as traced or allocated; only then can a figure be built up.

questions.q: Sewing thread used on hundreds of garment orders could be measured for each order, but weighing each cone every time would cost more than it is worth. In practice it is treated as…
options: An indirect cost, allocated to orders
questions.explain: Tracing is possible but not economically feasible, so the thread is allocated — the classic textbook example of an indirect material.

questions.q: A manager says the electricity cost of a dyeing order is ‘obviously’ Rs 50,000. What should the costing engineer ask?
options: Whether the figure is above budget
Whether it was traced from a meter on the machine or allocated on some base
Whether it was paid in cash
Whether the manager is senior enough
questions.explain: If the Rs 50,000 is an allocation, another base would give another number; if it was metered, it is a measurement. The lecture’s rule: traced or allocated?

questions.q: Which base does the lecture use to allocate pad-steam range depreciation to orders?
questions.explain: Depreciation is charged per machine-hour, since the range wears with the time it runs; steam is the cost allocated per metre.

questions.q: If the cost object is widened from the dyeing department to the whole mill, the dyeing manager’s salary becomes an indirect cost.
questions.explain: A wider cost object makes more costs traceable, not fewer; the salary is clearly a cost of the mill and remains direct to it.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Two-step allocations and the reasoning mistakes that make an allocated figure look like a fact.

questions.q: Why is ‘direct’ or ‘indirect’ not a fixed property of a cost?
options: Because it depends on the cost object chosen and on whether tracing is economically feasible
Because indirect costs are always fixed costs
questions.explain: The same supervisor’s salary is direct to a department and indirect to an order. Classification is a relationship between a cost and an object.

questions.q: Plant steam costs Rs 450,000 for 300,000 metres processed in all departments. The dyeing department processed 150,000 metres and then allocates its share per metre to orders. What steam cost reaches a 2,000-metre order?
Which costs in the lecture’s table are direct both to one dyeing order and to the dyeing department?
questions.explain: Fabric and dyes are issued or weighed for the order itself. Salary and depreciation are direct only to the department, and steam is indirect to both.

questions.q: A common mistake is to treat an allocated cost as if it were measured. What is the danger?
options: The figure will be too small
A different allocation base would give a different cost, so decisions may rest on an arbitrary number
Allocated costs are never real costs
The trial balance will not agree
questions.explain: Allocation is a convention; change the base from metres to machine-hours and the order’s cost changes. A decision-maker must know which figures are judgements.

questions.q: An order of 1,800 metres has grey fabric Rs 120,000 and dyes Rs 15,000. Steam is allocated at Rs 2 per metre and range depreciation at Rs 350 per machine-hour for 4 hours. What is the total cost of the order?
The mill changes its allocation base for overheads from metres to machine-hours. Which part of an order’s cost changes?
options: The whole cost, including traced items
questions.explain: Traced costs are measured on the order and do not depend on any base. Only the allocated shares move when the base moves.

questions.q: Cost accumulation takes place before cost assignment.
questions.explain: Costs are first collected by department, machine or account; only then can they be traced or allocated to cost objects.

questions.q: With the dyeing department as the cost object, which cost is still indirect?
questions.explain: Plant steam serves all departments and is allocated per department. The other three are traced to the dyeing department.

questions.q: An order’s direct cost is Rs 208,500 and its allocated costs are supervision Rs 4,200, steam Rs 7,500 and depreciation Rs 1,950. What percentage of the order’s total cost is allocated, to two decimal places?
questions.explain: Allocated = 13,650; total = 222,150; 13,650 ÷ 222,150 × 100 = 6.14 %, about 6.15 % after rounding of the intermediate figures.

questions.q: Which of these questions belongs to managerial rather than financial accounting?
options: What was the mill’s profit last year for the tax return?
What does one metre of dyed fabric for order 4471 cost us?
What did the balance sheet show the bank on 30 June?
How much is owed to creditors at year end?
questions.explain: The cost of a specific cost object is an inward-looking question for managers’ decisions. The other three are reports of past results to outsiders.
